newsitem.title: USA: Congress, Clinton head for disaster aid showdown.
newsitem.headline: Congress, Clinton head for disaster aid showdown.

text.p: Congress passed an $8.6 billion disaster relief bill Thursday, providing aid to 35 states and money for U.S. troops abroad, and sent it on to a threatened veto by President Clinton.
The Senate passed the emergency spending bill on a vote of 67 to 31 and it passed the House on a largely party-line vote of 220 to 201.
The president has vowed to veto the bill as soon as it reaches his desk. Assuming Clinton carries out his threat, Congress will not be back in session to act on a revised version until Tuesday.
The bill:

-- provides $5.4 billion for disaster assistance to 35 states hit by floods, winter storms and tornados. Some of those most in need are in the upper Midwest. Local officials there said this week that an early winter could curtail the time available for recovery from the flood.
-- repays $1.9 billion toward the cost of keeping U.S. troops in Bosnia and the Gulf.
-- contains $262 million for feeding poor women and their children, for education and for a new transportation system at Yosemite National Park.

Republican leaders of both the House and Senate refused to remove two provisions Clinton has said he will not accept -- the first to avert another government shutdown and the second to block the use of statistical sampling in the 2000 census.

Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott said he will call the president's bluff on the disaster assistance and assumed the president will sign the bill despite repeated insistance by Clinton and his aides that it will be vetoed.

"Sometimes you threaten things you don't actually do. Sometimes you are bluffing," the Mississippi Republican said at a news conference. He added that if it is vetoed, the next version will contain similar provisions.

House Appropriations Committee chairman Bob Livingston, Republican of Louisiana, said neither issue was worth a fight. "My advice to the president is 'sign the bill and we'll be through.' These are not life and death issues."

Clinton issued a statement Thursday night making clear the bill was doomed. "By attaching a political wish list to the much-needed disaster relief legislation, the congressional majority has chosen politics over the public interest."
He called on "the Republican leaders of Congress to keep ... politics off disaster relief legislation" and send him a disaster aid bill without unrelated conditions.

Once Clinton has vetoed the disaster bill, it was expected to make a quick U-turn back to Capitol Hill. A House Republican source said the two Republican-backed provisions would be stripped from the bill and it would be sent back to him for his signature, but Livingston said strategy will be mapped out Tuesday morning when the House returns.
Lott outlined a different scenario: "Census language and anti-government shutdown language will be in this bill."
"The president doesn't get everything just the way he wants it," he added.

Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle, whose state of South Dakota needs relief funds, predicted a swift turnaround. "My hope is the Republicans will keep the car running. Because it isn't going to take long to turn this car around, bring the bill back here, strip out the language."

Republicans sought to use the must-pass disaster relief bill to prevent that from happening again this fall. They proposed to continue spending past the Oct. 1 start of the new fiscal year, whether or not money bills have been passed.
But Democrats and the administration objected that this would give Republicans no incentive to negotiate with them on regular spending bills.

On the census issue, the parties were divided. Republicans were generally eager to keep the traditional house-by-house count used for decades. Democrats, who generally had greater representation among minorities, and Republicans in Texas and states with large minority populations approved use of sampling, a statistical procedure designed to adjust for undercounting minorities.
The Census Bureau, backed by a National Science Foundation study, said the sampling would provide a more accurate count of minorities.
